what_its_for: Apomorphine is used to treat sudden 'off' episodes in people with Parkinson's disease. 'Off' episodes are times when your Parkinson's symptoms suddenly come back or get worse, such as stiffness, tremors, or difficulty moving. This medicine works quickly to help you move more freely during these episodes.
how_to_take: Apomorphine comes in two forms: an injection you give yourself under the skin (subcutaneous injection), or a film that dissolves under your tongue (sublingual film). For the injection: inject it into your stomach, upper arm, or upper leg as directed by your doctor. Rotate injection sites each time. For the under-the-tongue film: place one film under your tongue and let it dissolve completely — do not chew, swallow, or eat or drink anything until it is fully dissolved. Always take apomorphine exactly as your doctor tells you. Do NOT take this medicine by vein (intravenously). Your doctor or nurse will show you how to use it before you try it on your own.
dosing: Your doctor will start you on a low dose and slowly increase it to find the right amount for you. The usual starting dose for the injection is 0.2 mL (2 mg) given under the skin when you have an 'off' episode. The dose may be slowly increased up to 0.6 mL (6 mg). For the under-the-tongue film, the usual starting dose is 10 mg. Your doctor may increase this up to 30 mg if needed. Do not use more than 5 doses in one day and wait at least 2 hours between doses. Never use more than your doctor prescribed.
missed_dose: Apomorphine is taken only when you are having an 'off' episode, not on a regular schedule. If you experience an 'off' episode and forget to use your apomorphine, use it as soon as you remember. Never use two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store apomorphine injections at room temperature between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from light and heat. Do not freeze it. Once you load the injection pen, use it within a certain number of days as instructed — check your product label. Store the under-the-tongue films at room temperature. Keep all apomorphine products out of reach of children. Throw away any unused or expired medicine safely — ask your pharmacist how.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while using apomorphine, as it can increase dizziness and the risk of fainting. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position, as this medicine can cause low blood pressure and make you feel faint or dizzy. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how this medicine affects you, as it can cause sudden sleepiness or drowsiness. Avoid medicines called 5-HT3 antagonists (such as ondansetron, granisetron, or dolasetron) — using them with apomorphine can cause a dangerous drop in blood pressure. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before taking any new medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or get emergency help if you experience: fainting or very low blood pressure, chest pain or fast/irregular heartbeat, unusual or uncontrollable movements (dyskinesias), confusion or hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there), sudden urge to fall asleep without warning, signs of skin problems or sores at the injection site, prolonged and painful erection (priapism), nausea or vomiting that is severe, or any signs of allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing.
when_it_works: Apomorphine works quickly. The injection usually starts working within 10 to 20 minutes of use. The under-the-tongue film typically starts working within about 15 to 35 minutes. The effects usually last for about 60 to 90 minutes. This medicine is not meant to replace your regular Parkinson's medicines — keep taking all your other medicines as prescribed.
special_populations: Older adults: Use with extra caution. Older adults are more likely to experience low blood pressure, dizziness, falls, and confusion. Start with the lowest dose. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It is not known if apomorphine is safe during pregnancy or passes into breast milk. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Children: Apomorphine is not approved for use in children.
